nodes.claim: "Some things are true and some are false — and I want to be able to tell which is which."
Discovering Reality
Building Confidence in Logical and Historical Claims
Defining God
Religious Comparison — Alignment with Reality
Historical Comparison — New Testament vs. Quran
Non-Fundamental Comparison — Christianity vs. Islam
Results and Conclusion
Phenomenological Grounding: "distinct things occur in my awareness."
Epistemological Grounding: information about phenomena can be identified, compared, and known.
Ontological Grounding: reality is what exists independently of want — including myself.
Logical Grounding: statements can be true or false, and new statements can be derived from existing ones.
Reasoning verifies whether a statement is true or not.
A method of reasoning that justifies falsehood can't distinguish it from truth.
"I want to know what is actually true — not what I want to be true."
Phenomena occur.
Distinct phenomena occur.
Qualities occur.
Associations occur.
Awareness is the occurrence of a quality or association.
Phenomena are identified by features and patterns.
A comparison is observing sameness or variation between information.
A match is sameness between compared information.
A mismatch is variation between compared information.
Phenomena are associated in distinct "types".
Questions result in knowledge or ignorance.
"All" of a class includes its instances in both knowledge and ignorance.
Information is a quality or association.
Information belongs with a phenomenon.
A feature is a distinct piece of information.
An identity is a set of features belonging to only one phenomenon.
Identification is the awareness of a phenomenon's identity.
A pattern is a similar quality that a set of features have.
Sameness is the similarity of a pattern across its features.
Variation is the difference of a pattern across its features.
A class is a similar quality that a set of patterns have.
Willful phenomena occur.
Intensities occur.
Temporal phenomena occur.
Physical phenomena occur.
Emotional phenomena occur.
Mental phenomena occur.
Relational phenomena occur.
Wantings occur.
Direction is the wanted information.
Success is the occurrence of what is wanted.
Failure is the non-occurrence of what is wanted.
An outcome is a success or failure.
Wanted wants occur.
A desire is an unwanted want.
A will is a wanted want.
Phenomena occur with intensity.
Sensation is intensity without wanting.
Perception is the occurrence of a sensation.
Satisfaction is when a wanted sensation occurs.
Frustration is when a wanted sensation does not occur.
Phenomena occur presently.
Past phenomena are those that occur before the present.
A memory is a present phenomenon about a past phenomenon.
Recognition is when a phenomenon is like a memory.
A phenomenon is new when it occurs without recognition.
Phenomena occur sequentially.
A step is a phenomenon in a sequence.
Change is the difference of a quality in a sequence.
An event is the transition from "not-occurring" to "occurring".
Imagination is information from different memories.
A visualization is the sensation of an imagination.
A thought is a set of imaginations and their associations.
A possibility is a thought that matches recognized patterns.
The future is a possibility of what occurs after the present.
A correlation is when one event often follows another.
An expectation is a possibility based on a correlation.
A hope is a possibility based on a want.
Independence is when the variations in one set of features do not correlate with the variations in another.
Consistency is sameness across a sequence.
A fundamental feature is one that is consistent.
A superficial feature is variation within a fundamental feature.
A cause is a want whose direction correlates with an event.
An effect is an event that correlates with a cause's direction.
A question is a want for specific information.
An answer is the occurrence of a question's wanted information.
Knowledge is when an answer occurs.
Ignorance is when an answer does not occur.
Learning is the change from ignorance to knowledge.
Forgetting is the change from knowledge to ignorance.
Phenomena occur independently from want — a limit.
Nature is the set of features for a limit.
A structure is a set of limits.
Ontological Bridge: objects exist independently of observation and want.
Reality is all objects.
A relationship is an association between objects.
"I am an object in reality."
Outcomes do not correlate with want.
Wants do not correlate with sensations.
What is thought about is independent from what occurs.
A limit is what is independent from want.
An object is a structure with nature.
Existence is the occurrence of an object.
An observation is the perception of an object.
New objects appear in observation.
An object's nature is consistent across observations.
An object's nature is independent from its observation.
Not all objects are currently observed.
"I" is the object that will is.
"My body is the object that my will affects."
"Not all of my body's events are caused by my will."
"My body limits my will."
"I am not my body."
Statements about reality are true or false, and are held as beliefs.
Concepts have rationality and comprehensibility, and are either compatible or contradictory.
Rationality and comprehensibility are independent, and truth corresponds with rationality.
A statement's truth depends on others.
Valid arguments derive new statements, including about what is not observed.
An abstraction is information about a pattern or class.
Descriptions are either true or false.
A statement is a description about reality.
Evidence is an observation that matches or mismatches what a statement describes.
A belief is a statement thought to be true.
An assumption is a belief without evidence.
A judgment is a belief with evidence.
A description is information about an object.
A definition is a description of an identity.
Descriptions match or mismatch what they describe.
A description is independent from what it describes.
Truth is when a description matches reality.
Falsehood is when a description mismatches reality.
A concept is a set of definitions.
Compatibility is when imagining a concept's definitions results in a visualization.
A contradiction is when imagining a concept's definitions does not result in a visualization.
A concept is rational when its definitions are compatible.
A concept is comprehensible when imagining its object results in a visualization.
A concept is either rational or irrational.
A concept is either comprehensible or incomprehensible.
A concept's rationality is independent from its comprehensibility.
Some concepts are rational and comprehensible.
Some concepts are irrational yet comprehensible.
Some concepts are rational yet incomprehensible.
Some concepts are irrational and incomprehensible.
Truth corresponds with rationality, not comprehensibility.
A possible statement is one that does not contradict what is known.
An impossible statement is one that contradicts what is known.
A dependency is when one statement's truth or falsehood contradicts another's.
A statement is necessary for another when its falsehood contradicts the other's truth.
A statement is sufficient for another when its truth contradicts the other's falsehood.
A condition is a statement that is necessary or sufficient for another.
An implication is the relationship between a sufficient statement and what it is sufficient for.
A premise is a statement from which an implication follows.
A conclusion is a statement that an implication leads to.
An argument is a set of premises and their conclusion.
An argument is valid when its premises are sufficient for its conclusion.
A derivation is the conclusion of a valid argument.
A justification is a valid argument whose conclusion is a belief.
Unobserved derivations occur from valid arguments.
An inference is a new statement that results from other statements or observations.
Induction is an inference from a pattern in observations to an abstraction.
Deduction is an inference from premises through valid implication.
A deduction is sound when its premises are true.
Verification is comparing a derivation against observation.
A prediction is a derivation about what is not yet observed.
A proof is a sequence of sound deductions from premises to a conclusion.
A process is a sequence where each step depends on the one before it.
A method is a class of processes.
Reasoning is the method of observation → identification → induction → deduction → verification.
A hope about something false can occur.
An assumption about something false can occur.
The outcome of reasoning can be false.
A method of reasoning that justifies falsehood is independent from truth.
Truth and falsehood lack distinction in a method of reasoning that is independent from truth.
